---
order: 3
unit: together
title: Pause before you post
summary: "Group chats move fast, and a message read without a face or a voice can land harder than it was meant. A short pause helps: read it as the other person would, ask whether you would say it to their face, and choose a kinder version or not sending at all. When a chat turns on someone, you can stay out of it, support them privately and tell an adult."
language: science
shape: 5e
hook: "In the class group chat, someone posts 'lol look at Sam's haircut'. Three people add laughing faces in ten seconds. What happens next?"
---
Everyone here is made up, and so is the group chat. Nobody needs to say what happens in their own chats.

## Engage: how does it land?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess: the sender knows what they meant, but the reader only sees the words."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Ruby types 'nice drawing 🙄' to Leo as a joke between friends. How might Leo read it?"
  options: ["As mean: he can't see her smile or hear her tone", "As a joke: Ruby meant it as one", "He won't notice the emoji"]
  actual: "He might read it as mean. A message has no face and no voice. What Ruby meant does not travel with the words."
```

## Explore: kinder or harder?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting real-feeling replies shows that small changes in words change how a message lands."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Jo shares a video of her first try at skateboarding in the group. Is each reply kind, or likely to hurt?"
  options: ["Kind", "Likely to hurt"]
  items:
    - ["You stayed on way longer than I would 😄", "Kind", "It laughs with Jo, not at her."]
    - ["LOL fail", "Likely to hurt", "Short, public and about her falling."]
    - ["Brave! Show us the next try?", "Kind", "It notices the effort."]
    - ["Someone send this to the whole year 😂", "Likely to hurt", "It asks to make the audience bigger without asking Jo."]
    - ["(no reply)", "Kind", "Not replying is fine. Nobody has to add to every message."]
    - ["Sending her a private 'that was cool' instead of posting in the group", "Kind", "Support doesn't have to be public."]
```

Was your guess right? The same moment can get a kind reply or a hard one. **What lands is the words, not what was meant.**

## Explain: the pause

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Three questions make a pause. The planted mistake is judging a message by what the sender meant."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#ari"
      text: "Ari adds to a group chat. Click the line where his thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: joke-is-fine-if-meant
      explain: "Line 2: Ari decides it's fine because he means it as a joke. Sam only sees the words, from several people, in front of the whole group."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Ari wants to show he is on Sam's side without making things worse in the group. What could he do?"
      options: ["Send Sam a private message to check he is OK", "Post 'stop being mean' and tag everyone", "Leave the group without saying anything", "Screenshot the chat and post it somewhere else"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Speaking up can help, but tagging everyone can make the pile-on bigger. A private message is a safe first step.", "Leaving is fine for Ari, but Sam still doesn't know anyone cares.", "That spreads the hurtful message further."]
      explain: "A private message to Sam supports him without adding to the group. Telling an adult is the next step if it keeps going."
```

Before you send, **pause** and ask:

1. **How will they read it?** Read it as the other person, with no face and no voice.
2. **Would I say it to their face?** If not, don't type it.
3. **Is there a kinder version, or is no reply better?** Both are good choices.

When a chat turns on someone, you have choices too: don't add to it, check on them privately, and tell a trusted adult if it keeps going. Everyone sends something they regret sometimes. Saying sorry and fixing it is part of the habit.

## Elaborate: when the chat is bigger

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Years 7 and 8: bigger chats, screenshots and pressure to join in; the same pause, plus what a bystander can do."
check:
  type: question
  q: "In a year-group chat of 80 people, someone posts an embarrassing screenshot of a private message Mei sent. Most people are reacting. What is the best thing to do?"
  options: ["Don't react or share, check on Mei privately, and tell a trusted adult", "React too, so you don't stand out", "Reply with a joke to change the subject", "Forward it to Mei so she knows"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Reacting adds to it, even if you don't mean it.", "That leaves the screenshot there and may add to it.", "Mei may already know, and getting it again can hurt more. Ask her how she is instead."]
  explain: "Not adding to it, a private check-in and telling a trusted adult are the bystander's three moves. An adult can help get it taken down."
```

## Evaluate: a kinder version

```step
stage: info
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which is the kinder version of 'ur project is so boring'?"
      options: ["'I liked the pictures. Maybe a bit shorter?'", "'ur project is so boring lol'", "'boring'", "'everyone thinks ur project is boring'"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Adding lol doesn't change how it lands.", "Shorter, but still hurtful.", "Adding everyone makes it worse."]
      explain: "It notices something good and makes one suggestion."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can use the pause: how will they read it, would I say it to their face, is there a kinder version?" }
```

### Look back

**A private think** (just for you): which of the three pause questions would help you most?

```teacher
summary: "Students predict how a joking message lands, sort replies to a
  friend's video as kind or likely to hurt, find the mistake in judging a
  message by what was meant, and learn a three-question pause plus what a
  bystander can do. Typical width (Years 7 and 8): a screenshot in a big
  year-group chat."
time: 40
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 12 min · Elaborate 8 min · Evaluate 10 min
goals:
  - I can explain why a message can land harder than it was meant.
  - I can use a pause before I send.
  - I can say what I could do when a chat turns on someone.
struggle: Students defend jokes ('it was only a joke'). Agree that it may have
  been meant as one, then ask what the reader could see.
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this lesson touches on group-chat unkindness and
  bullying, so it is especially worth reading with the school's wellbeing lead
  before teaching. Agree the support pathway and any local wording, and align it
  with the school's bullying policy and reporting process.


  **If a student discloses something:** follow the school's child-protection
  procedure (and the bullying policy where it applies). Listen, don't probe,
  don't promise to keep it secret, and pass it on as the procedure says. Thank
  them and steer the class back to Ari and Sam.


  **Ground rules:** Ari, Sam, Ruby, Leo, Jo and Mei are made up. Never ask
  whether this has happened in the class's own chats or to anyone they know, and
  don't ask for examples. Some students may be on either side of something like
  this right now: watch for distress, and avoid blame. The message is "a pause
  and a kinder choice help", not "you are bad if you did this". The closing
  think is private.


  No laws are stated. For reporting serious online bullying, point to the
  school's process first, then the eSafety Commissioner (esafety.gov.au/report).


  Years 5 and 6: give the link with `?width=minimum` to hide the year-group chat
  scenario.
running:
  - "Engage: read Ruby's message aloud in two different tones. Which one does
    Leo get?"
  - "Explore: ask why '(no reply)' counts as kind."
  - "Explain: put the three pause questions on the board; leave them up for the
    rest of the course."
  - "Elaborate (Years 7 and 8): name the bystander's three moves."
  - "Evaluate: pairs write their own kinder version of a made-up message, on
    paper, not shared with the class."
stuck:
  - see: A student insists it was only a joke.
    ask: "What could Sam see: the joke, or the words?"
    fix: What was meant doesn't travel. Read it as the other person.
  - see: A student thinks the only choices are join in or fight back.
    ask: What could you do that nobody else in the chat sees?
    fix: Don't add to it, check on them privately, tell a trusted adult.
  - see: A student becomes upset or starts talking about a real chat.
    ask: (Don't probe.) Acknowledge it quietly, and offer to talk after class.
    fix: Follow up privately and through the wellbeing team or the bullying policy.
stretch: Rewrite Ari's message so it is a joke Sam would laugh at too, or decide
  it can't be done. Why?
support: The three pause questions on a card on the desk.
leads: >
  Next: who is on the other end? Not everyone online is who they say.


  Links: AI in your life › A fake about someone (Years 7 and up; bystanders and
  reporting when a fake is shared).
exit:
  q: Name one thing a bystander can do when a group chat turns on someone.
  a: Not add to it, check on them privately, or tell a trusted adult.
explain: >
  A message has **no face and no voice**. What you meant doesn't travel with the
  words.


  Before you send, **pause**: How will they read it? Would I say it to their
  face? Is there a kinder version, or is no reply better?


  When a chat turns on someone: don't add to it, check on them privately, and
  tell a trusted adult if it keeps going.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Ari says, 'I was only joking, so it's not my fault Sam left.' Is he right?
    prompts:
      - Does what you meant matter? Does what they felt matter more?
      - What could Ari do now to fix it?
    notes: Both matter, but the reader only has the words. Fixing it (saying sorry,
      checking on Sam) is part of the habit. Keep it about Ari.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Two tones
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Your teacher reads "nice drawing 🙄" twice, in two different voices.
        Which one would Leo hear in his head?
      notes: Read it once warmly, once sarcastically. Text carries neither.
    - at: end
      kind: activity
      title: Kinder versions
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        In pairs, rewrite these made-up messages so they are kind, or decide no
        reply is best: "that's so cringe", "why would u even post that",
        "everyone's talking about you".
      notes: Paper only; don't collect or read them out unless a pair offers. Accept
        'no reply' as a strong answer.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: The pause
      type: question
      q: Which pause question catches a message that's fine to say out loud, but not
        in text?
      options:
        - How will they read it?
        - Would I say it to their face?
        - Is it a good joke?
      answer: 0
      explain: Without a voice or a face, even a friendly line can be read the wrong
        way.
```

Ari thinks: I'm only joking, so it's fine if I add one too.
He posts "haha did his little brother cut it?"
Two more people join in, and Sam leaves the group.
